headline: Christina Applegate feels like 'fraud' after MS misdiagnosis
subheadline: Christina Applegate reflects on Multiple Sclerosis misdiagnosis
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Christina Applegate has said she feels like a “fraud” after learning she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, admitting she is “back at square one” in understanding her health.

The Dead to Me star, 54, spoke on her podcast MeSsy, which she co-hosts with Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

On the latest episode, recorded with guest Jack Osbourne, she joked: “Talk about being a fraud, I don’t even have it anymore, jeez.”

Read more: Christina Applegate feels she's 'let everybody down' after MS misdiagnosis

Applegate first revealed the misdiagnosis on the 20 October episode, saying she felt she had “let everybody down.”

She said she lived as a person with MS for almost six years, having announced her diagnosis in August 2021 while filming the third and final series of Dead to Me.

She has stressed that the news does not mean everything is resolved.

“This may come as great news, but to me, I’m back at square one,” she said. She added: “You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden I’m better.”

Applegate is now being tested for conditions with similar symptoms, including rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and Lyme disease.

“So now I’m being tested for all that stuff, slowly but surely,” she said. No results have been shared.

She said the situation has left her more frustrated than relieved, and that she is still adjusting to this change in her health journey.

She also wants to stay involved in the MS community. “I’m still always going to be a part of it,” she said.

Osbourne, 45, who lives with MS, said he sometimes feels like a fraud himself, though his condition “hasn’t stopped me”.

Sigler, also 45, made Applegate an “honorary member” of the MS community, and Osbourne offered to send her some resources, which she said she appreciated.

Read more: Christina Applegate speaks out after 'misdiagnosed'

headline: King Charles reveals special island-inspired setting for royal dinner
subheadline: Royal watchers await for King Charles and Queen Camilla’s grand arrival
author: Web Desk
article_text:
King Charles and Queen Camilla are preparing to welcome Commonwealth leaders to a dinner in Antigua.

The Royal Family shared a BTS look at the preparations, sharing photographs of the beautifully arranged tables ahead of Tuesday evening’s official of Government dinner.

The table setting was a blend of island charm and royal tradition, with colourful checked tablecloths and napkins, floral arrangements and candle lanterns bringing warmth to the tables.

Palm trees and a sweeping coastal view provided a beautiful backdrop for the occasion.

Royal editor Rebecca English was equally taken with the preparations, sharing her own preview of the evening with followers.

"What a night! A preview of tonight's dinner thrown by the King features breathtaking Caribbean produce with a Buckingham Palace twist," she wrote.

She also noticed the locally made table mats, created by Antiguan artisan 'Sexy Sue', and a special cocktail named 'Commonwealth 56' – a nod to the organisation's 56 member countries.

headline: US midterms: Ossoff defeats rival to retain key Georgia Senate seat for Democrats
subheadline: A Democratic Senate majority would give the party greater power to scrutinise Trump's administration
author: Reuters
article_text:
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won reelection in Georgia on Tuesday, according to media projections, defeating President Donald Trump-backed Republican US Representative Mike Collins and preserving a crucial seat as Democrats seek to regain control of the Senate.

Ossoff's victory in one of the country's most closely contested Senate races marks an important win for Democrats in a state Trump carried by two percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.

It also keeps the party's hopes of securing a Senate majority alive as results come in from across the country.

The senator, widely viewed as a potential contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, raised $126 million more than Collins during the campaign.

Collins, meanwhile, benefited from $18 million in outside spending after emerging from a three-way Republican primary and subsequent runoff.

Trump had endorsed Collins over former college football coach Derek Dooley, who had the backing of outgoing Republican Governor Brian Kemp.

Republicans entered Tuesday's elections with a 53-47 majority in the Senate, meaning Democrats needed a net gain of four seats to take control of the chamber.

Georgia was among the seats Democrats had to defend to have a realistic chance of achieving that goal.

Their path also depended on retaining a seat in Michigan and defeating Republican incumbents in Maine and North Carolina, while making further gains in states Trump won by double-digit margins in 2024, including Ohio, Alaska, Iowa and Texas.

A Democratic Senate majority would give the party greater influence over legislation and the confirmation of senior government appointments, while making it harder for Trump to advance his agenda during the remainder of his presidency.

headline: Colman Domingo reveals Hollywood Superstar he attended high school with
subheadline: Colman Domingo recalls going to high school with 'cool kid' A-lister
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Colman Domingo has revealed that he went to high school in Philadelphia with Will Smith, describing the future superstar as “the cool kid” while he was “the nerd.”

The Euphoria and Sing Sing actor, 56, shared the memory on Tuesday’s episode of the video podcast Friends Keep Secrets, hosted by Benny Blanco, Lil Dicky and Kristin Batalucco.

The pair attended Overbrook High School, with Smith, now 58, a year ahead.

Read more: Colman Domingo recalls emotional bond with late Chadwick Boseman

They shared a few classes. “We had gym class and science class together,” Domingo said.

He recalled that Smith was already popular at school and was performing locally with DJ Jazzy Jeff.

“All the cool kids went to see them,” he said. Domingo did not go along to the shows, explaining that he “wasn’t a cool kid.” The two were not friends.

Their paths crossed again years later.

Domingo said he was working as a waiter at El Torito in Philadelphia when Smith, by then hugely successful in music and acting, came in.

Smith did not recognise him at first, but once his memory was jogged, the pair hugged.

Domingo said he had never bumped into Smith during their careers, and hopes they will meet again, given their shared Philadelphia roots.

On the work front, Domingo’s projects include An Innocent Girl, The Comebacker and the Netflix comedy series The Four Seasons.

Smith is set to appear in the action thriller Supermax.

The Euphoria and Sing Sing actor, 56, shared the memory on Tuesday’s episode of the video podcast Friends Keep Secrets, hosted by Benny Blanco, Lil Dicky and Kristin Batalucco. 

The pair attended Overbrook High School, with Smith, now 58, a year ahead.

Read more: Colman Domingo recalls emotional bond with late Chadwick Boseman

They shared a few classes. “We had gym class and science class together,” Domingo said.

He recalled that Smith was already popular at school and was performing locally with DJ Jazzy Jeff. 

“All the cool kids went to see them,” he said. Domingo did not go along to the shows, explaining that he “wasn’t a cool kid.” The two were not friends.

Their paths crossed again years later. 

Domingo said he was working as a waiter at El Torito in Philadelphia when Smith, by then hugely successful in music and acting, came in.

Smith did not recognise him at first, but once his memory was jogged, the pair hugged.

Domingo said he had never bumped into Smith during their careers, and hopes they will meet again, given their shared Philadelphia roots.

On the work front, Domingo’s projects include An Innocent Girl, The Comebacker and the Netflix comedy series The Four Seasons. 

Smith is set to appear in the action thriller Supermax.

Read more: 'Michael' star Colman Domingo shares heartfelt tribute to late parents

headline: Jennifer Lawrence urges fans to vote in 'Hunger Games' style
subheadline: Jennifer Lawrence gives Katniss three-finger salute on Midterms Election Day
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Jennifer Lawrence has used a famous Hunger Games line to urge her fans to vote in the US midterm elections.

The Oscar winner shared a photo on her new Instagram page on Tuesday 3 November, Election Day, captioned: “MIDTERMS BB. DON’T FORGET WHO BURNS WITH US.”

The post included a link to information about polling places.

Read more: Jennifer Lawrence honest take on post-baby body changes

The picture shows Lawrence out and about in New York, wearing an oversized graphic T-shirt, a blue coat and red trousers.

She had her hair in a braid, the signature style of Katniss Everdeen, and gave the three-finger salute from the series, the silent symbol of rebellion that fans know well.

The caption echoes Katniss’s rally cry in the third film, when she warns the Capitol and President Snow: “Do you see that? Fire is catching... And if we burn, you burn with us!”

The post lands as the franchise prepares to return to cinemas.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the prequel based on Suzanne Collins’ bestselling novel, opens later this month.

Lawrence has also recently confirmed rumours that she will reprise Katniss, alongside Josh Hutcherson and Woody Harrelson, in scenes that are expected to adapt the book’s epilogue.

For many fans, the Election Day message was a reminder of how powerfully the series’ imagery of resistance and solidarity has endured since the first film.

Lawrence’s playful use of it kept the call to vote simple, and gave followers a quick nudge to head to the polls.

Read more: Jennifer Lawrence rules out her probablity of returning to 'X-Men'

headline: Cher reacts to Michael Douglas shading her 1988 Oscar win
subheadline: Michael Douglas said Glenn Close 'should have won' over Cher in 1988
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Cher has responded, through her representative, after Michael Douglas suggested that Glenn Close should have beaten her to the Best Actress Oscar in 1988.

“Cher adores Michael Douglas,” a spokesperson told Entertainment Weekly by email. The star herself did not comment directly.

Douglas made the remark on The Graham Norton Show last week, while appearing alongside Close.

Read more: Cher delivers powerful acceptance speech at Grammys 2026

Discussing Fatal Attraction, he said: “She should have won with Fatal Attraction.” When Norton replied “Oh, wow,” Douglas quipped: “I know, that’s what we all said.” Close cut in with, “Michael, be kind!”

Cher won Best Actress at the 60th Academy Awards for Moonstruck, while Close was nominated for her performance as Alex Forrest in Fatal Attraction.

Douglas himself won Best Actor that night for Wall Street.

Fatal Attraction earned six nominations, including Best Picture, Best Supporting Actress for Anne Archer and Best Director for Adrian Lyne, but did not win any.

Douglas noted that the 1988 nomination was, by his count, Close’s fourth since 1983. Cher had also been nominated that year for Best Supporting Actress, for Silkwood.

The comments come at a notable time for Close, who is due to receive her first Honorary Award from the Academy days after the interview. She has been nominated eight times without winning a competitive Oscar.

Douglas also told Norton that the Fatal Attraction team initially had doubts about casting Close as Alex Forrest, and that she won the part after her agent pushed for her to be given an audition.

Read more: Oscar winner Michael Douglas looks back on secret romance with co-star

headline: Hailey Bieber opens up about health battle following son Jack's birth
subheadline: Hailey Bieber says talking about PMDD makes it 'less of a lonely journey'
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Hailey Bieber has revealed that she struggled with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) after the birth of her son, Jack Blues, saying that open conversation helps make it “less of a lonely journey.”

The Rhode founder, who is married to Justin Bieber, told WWD that the condition affected her after Jack was born in August 2024.

“After I had my son, I struggled with [PMDD] a bit, and there’s just not a lot of conversation or research around it,” she said.

Read more: Hailey Bieber reveals future family plans with Justin Bieber

PMDD is a severe form of premenstrual syndrome, and symptoms can include anxiety, panic attacks, depression, insomnia, fatigue and mood swings.

Bieber explained why she chose to speak out, saying that talking about it helps people feel less alone and “makes it feel like less of a lonely journey.”

The comments follow other health revelations she made on the Therapuss podcast earlier this year.

She said she had a “mini stroke” in 2022, adding: “A couple of years ago, I had a crazy medical situation.”

She also explained that she was born with a heart defect, a patent foramen ovale, which required surgery carried out through the groin. She was able to go in and out of hospital on the same day.

The experience left her feeling “hyper aware” of her body, she said, and contributed to her anxiety.

Bieber says her interest in health and medicine helped inspire her beauty brand, Rhode.

The company has pledged $5 million to the Foundation for Women’s Health over three years to support research into women’s health. She sold Rhode to e.l.f. Beauty in 2025 for $1 billion.

Read more: Hailey Bieber shares hilarious meme featuring Justin Bieber

headline: Hilary Duff recalls dumping tuna wieners on boy's lawn
subheadline: Hilary Duff confesses to 'kind of evil' teenage prank
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Hilary Duff has revealed her “spiciest” memory, a teenage prank in which she and her friends emptied a can of tuna and wieners on the front lawn of a boy who had treated one of them badly.

The singer and actress, 39, shared the story during Billboard’s Take Me Out video series, which was released on Tuesday 3 November.

“This guy was doing my friend real dirty and we were hitting the bottle,” she said.

Read more: Hilary Duff on Lizzie McGuire: 'I'm never singing that song'

She and her friends then “bought the cheapest, grossest can of wieners and tuna” and “had a little field day on his front lawn.”

Duff said the incident happened in her “late teen-hood” and described herself as “really not a big goer-outer.”

She called the prank “kind of evil” and said it was “a long time ago, pre-children.”

The video comes as Duff is busy with music.

Her single CATastrophe, released last month for the Cat in the Hat soundtrack, has a music video, and the film opens on Friday 6 November.

Her album Luck... or Something came out in February.

Her Lucky Me Tour has also been extended into 2027, with 32 new dates across Europe, Latin America and the United States, running through late 2027.

The updated schedule includes a stop in Milan.

The prank story is the latest example of the playful, self-deprecating tone Duff has become known for, and fans will be watching to see whether she brings any more tales of her wilder days to the road.

headline: War of words
subheadline: Fazl's initial trigger came with language mainstream parents would prefer not to teach their children at home
author: Farhan Bokhari
article_text:
The war of words triggered in the past week between Maulana Fazlur Rehman and Pakistan’s ministers of defence and interior unleashed another visible drama at the centre of the country’s politics. But eventually, this episode too promises to go down in history as another hollow ring.

In time, the occasion will become a powerful reminder of a representative structure that remains detached from Pakistan’s compelling realities, with most of the country’s population facing fast-mounting challenges elsewhere. With the lives of Pakistan’s vast community of the disfranchised continuing without hope for the foreseeable future, the political elite remaining locked in this latest crossfire keeps them detached from the grassroots.

Against this backdrop, it would have been far more meaningful for members of the ruling structure and their political foes to lock horns and debate matters that have increasingly triggered the multiple crises facing the people of Pakistan. Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s initial trigger came with language mainstream parents would prefer not to teach their children at home. With much that Maulana Fazlur Rehman needs to be accounted for from his own past, taking the moral high ground in the name of protecting Pakistan’s democracy was just not his choice. His opponents from Pakistan’s ruling structure, with equally chequered histories, quickly found ammunition to respond in kind and more.

The ongoing circus at the centre of Pakistan’s highest political landscape comes at a deeply inopportune moment for the country’s present and future. It follows the recently reported hike in inflation fuelled by mounting fuel and food prices, which last week compelled the State Bank of Pakistan to raise its interest rates by 0.5% to 12%.

The central bank’s choice was a powerful reminder that Pakistan’s mainstream population is bearing the brunt of worsening times. The fallout from that trend has already hit hard the average household budgets, including large parts of the middle class once considered relatively immune from previous episodes of a slumping economy.

Pakistan’s political turmoil, unleashed in recent times over controversy surrounding the conduct of the 2024 election, of course remains unending. And reversing that turmoil requires undoing all that has fuelled the rot. In this journey, the federal government’s recent decision to impose a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has only added fuel to the proverbial fire that represents Pakistan’s politics today. Without resolving Pakistan’s fast-growing political discord, the country will not achieve the peace needed to recover other essential areas, notably the economy.

While Pakistan’s internal discord continues, the government and the opposition must cope with two equally essential challenges. First, the economic challenges confronting Pakistan today include alarming issues at the centre of the country’s survival. These include galloping inflation and risks tied to worsening climate change, deepening the malaise of a visibly moribund economy. For now, these challenges have kept investors – foreign and domestic – averse to becoming exposed to investing in Pakistan, notably for the long haul. This mood represents a formidable departure from eras like the 1960s when Pakistan was considered a destination of choice for investors.

The prevailing mood among investors has also been fuelled by other factors, notably the shrinking pool of well-trained labourers to meet the needs of businesses and industries. This is the tragic outcome of previous decades, spent with Pakistan’s educational system becoming increasingly neglected, barring a few notable institutions. Though successive governments have relentlessly pursued Pakistan’s labour export and the resulting inflow of foreign remittances, they have largely ignored the downside risk in this journey. That failure is not to build a pool of well-trained labourers to meet the needs of economic growth in new ventures at home.

Second, Pakistan’s domestic insecurity today continues on many fronts. These are not all just the threats from the Taliban operating from Afghanistan. Though the threat of the Taliban onslaught must never be overlooked, insecurity elsewhere cannot be ignored either. From large, thriving urban centres to every corner of Pakistan’s rural areas, insecurity is visibly growing and needs urgent attention. Even the ongoing debate over the creation of many more provinces has failed to address a fundamental question. How will such reform address the gaps in security, beyond arming the visible political elite with authority at the grassroots? That remains an unanswered question.

Besides, there is no reconciliation yet with visibly failed past reforms, notably the dismantling of the civil service at the grassroots in the name of devolution, as pursued under the rule of the late president Gen Pervez Musharraf.

Beyond the ongoing political discord, much remains to be addressed to create a new Pakistan, not just the outcome of the ongoing infighting.

The writer is an Islamabad-based journalist who writes on political and economic affairs. He can be reached at: [email protected]

cleaned_text:
The war of words triggered in the past week between Maulana Fazlur Rehman and Pakistan’s ministers of defence and interior unleashed another visible drama at the centre of the country’s politics. But eventually, this episode too promises to go down in history as another hollow ring.

In time, the occasion will become a powerful reminder of a representative structure that remains detached from Pakistan’s compelling realities, with most of the country’s population facing fast-mounting challenges elsewhere. With the lives of Pakistan’s vast community of the disfranchised continuing without hope for the foreseeable future, the political elite remaining locked in this latest crossfire keeps them detached from the grassroots.

Against this backdrop, it would have been far more meaningful for members of the ruling structure and their political foes to lock horns and debate matters that have increasingly triggered the multiple crises facing the people of Pakistan. Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s initial trigger came with language mainstream parents would prefer not to teach their children at home. With much that Maulana Fazlur Rehman needs to be accounted for from his own past, taking the moral high ground in the name of protecting Pakistan’s democracy was just not his choice. His opponents from Pakistan’s ruling structure, with equally chequered histories, quickly found ammunition to respond in kind and more.

The ongoing circus at the centre of Pakistan’s highest political landscape comes at a deeply inopportune moment for the country’s present and future. It follows the recently reported hike in inflation fuelled by mounting fuel and food prices, which last week compelled the State Bank of Pakistan to raise its interest rates by 0.5% to 12%.

The central bank’s choice was a powerful reminder that Pakistan’s mainstream population is bearing the brunt of worsening times. The fallout from that trend has already hit hard the average household budgets, including large parts of the middle class once considered relatively immune from previous episodes of a slumping economy.

Pakistan’s political turmoil, unleashed in recent times over controversy surrounding the conduct of the 2024 election, of course remains unending. And reversing that turmoil requires undoing all that has fuelled the rot. In this journey, the federal government’s recent decision to impose a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has only added fuel to the proverbial fire that represents Pakistan’s politics today. Without resolving Pakistan’s fast-growing political discord, the country will not achieve the peace needed to recover other essential areas, notably the economy.

While Pakistan’s internal discord continues, the government and the opposition must cope with two equally essential challenges. First, the economic challenges confronting Pakistan today include alarming issues at the centre of the country’s survival. These include galloping inflation and risks tied to worsening climate change, deepening the malaise of a visibly moribund economy. For now, these challenges have kept investors – foreign and domestic – averse to becoming exposed to investing in Pakistan, notably for the long haul. This mood represents a formidable departure from eras like the 1960s when Pakistan was considered a destination of choice for investors.

The prevailing mood among investors has also been fuelled by other factors, notably the shrinking pool of well-trained labourers to meet the needs of businesses and industries. This is the tragic outcome of previous decades, spent with Pakistan’s educational system becoming increasingly neglected, barring a few notable institutions. Though successive governments have relentlessly pursued Pakistan’s labour export and the resulting inflow of foreign remittances, they have largely ignored the downside risk in this journey. That failure is not to build a pool of well-trained labourers to meet the needs of economic growth in new ventures at home.

Second, Pakistan’s domestic insecurity today continues on many fronts. These are not all just the threats from the Taliban operating from Afghanistan. Though the threat of the Taliban onslaught must never be overlooked, insecurity elsewhere cannot be ignored either. From large, thriving urban centres to every corner of Pakistan’s rural areas, insecurity is visibly growing and needs urgent attention. Even the ongoing debate over the creation of many more provinces has failed to address a fundamental question. How will such reform address the gaps in security, beyond arming the visible political elite with authority at the grassroots? That remains an unanswered question.

Besides, there is no reconciliation yet with visibly failed past reforms, notably the dismantling of the civil service at the grassroots in the name of devolution, as pursued under the rule of the late president Gen Pervez Musharraf.

Beyond the ongoing political discord, much remains to be addressed to create a new Pakistan, not just the outcome of the ongoing infighting.

headline: US midterms: Democrats retake control of Congress in sweeping setback for Trump
subheadline: Voters in conservative bastions who propelled president to his second term in office swing towards Democrats
author: Reuters
article_text:
Democrats hold Senate seats in Georgia, New Hampshire.
Party flips Republican-held House seat in North Carolina.
White House official says mood around Trump was "defiant."

Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives on Tuesday, scoring sweeping victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to President Donald Trump.

Voters in conservative bastions who had propelled the president to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats, fueled by deep frustration over the unpopular war with Iran, anxiety over the high cost of living and anger at Trump's stewardship of the country.

In Texas, the biggest Republican state, Democrats ended a decades-long losing streak in seismic fashion, winning a Senate seat and ousting three-term Governor Greg Abbott.

Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since the Great Depression nearly a century ago, and in South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, Democrats turned aside his hand-picked Senate candidate.

The results will usher in a new era of divided government in Washington, following two years in which the Republican-controlled Congress rarely exercised its power to rein in Trump.

Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump's administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation. The Democratic Senate can block Trump's nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise.

"There is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America," said Chuck Schumer, the party's Senate minority leader. "Americans voted for change, and now Democrats must deliver."

Trump, who is barred by the US Constitution from seeking a third term, has exercised an iron grip on his party for most of the last decade. But the new balance of power in Washington may accelerate his lame-duck status, as attention turns toward the 2028 presidential race and potential successors begin competing for political influence in a post-Trump world.

Despite worries from Democrats that Trump might seek to overturn the election results, as he did in 2020, the president accepted the outcome, congratulating Democrats in an interview with Fox News. He also said he would work with Democrats on issues such as immigration, though he threatened to veto any "insane" bills they passed.

Democratic wave

Democrats focused their campaign on corruption and affordability, blaming Trump's tariff policy and the war with Iran for driving up costs while highlighting the billions of dollars the Trump family has made since he returned to the White House.

Republicans, led by Trump, attacked Democrats over culture war issues such as transgender rights while portraying their opponents as radical and extreme. But in poll after poll, voters made it clear they were far more concerned with pocketbook issues.

The Democratic wave flooded huge swaths of the country. Republicans lost ground in all but a handful of the approximately 2,100 counties where most votes had been counted, according to tallies compiled by Reuters and USA Today.

Democrats made gains in the richest counties and the poorest; in counties where more people have college degrees and where fewer do. Democrats' advances were particularly sharp in heavily Latino counties, including the border counties of Texas that shifted toward Trump in 2024 and the agricultural towns of the Kansas prairie.

In Seward County, Kansas, home to one of America's biggest beef processing plants and where about half of eligible voters are Hispanic, Democrat Adam Hamilton led incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall by 13 points, two years after Trump won the county by 39 points.

Democrats flipped more than two dozen House seats currently held by Republicans, locking in a majority. Democrats won all the closely contested House races that have been decided so far, and they won about a dozen races in districts that Trump won by double digits two years ago.

An unprecedented Republican gambit to redraw several House districts to make them more favourable largely failed, with Democrats hanging on to most of the targeted seats.

Midterm elections are typically seen as a referendum on the sitting president, and Trump did little to disabuse voters of that notion. In the campaign's final weeks, he held dozens of rallies, telling supporters repeatedly to "pretend I'm on the ballot."

He also intervened in several Republican primaries earlier this year to ensure his preferred candidates reached the ballot, despite concerns from some Republicans that his choices carried significant liabilities.

In Texas, Trump backed Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden state attorney general, over the incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. In South Carolina, the president anointed Darline Graham, a political neophyte, after her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, died suddenly earlier this year. Both candidates lost.

But even candidates who sought to distance themselves from Trump were unable to escape voters' wrath. In Maine, Republican incumbent Susan Collins had her 30-year Senate career end on Tuesday, despite emphasising her willingness to break with the president during the campaign.

Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s open Senate seat, becoming the first Muslim elected to the chamber. He defeated Mike Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent, who entered the race with Trump's backing and sought to falsely portray El-Sayed, an Egyptian American born in Michigan, as a religious extremist.

"You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope," El-Sayed told cheering supporters on Tuesday night, referring to Rogers.

Competitive Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska had yet to be called early on Wednesday.

On Tuesday night, as it grew clear Republicans were in danger of losing their congressional majorities, Trump wrote on social media, "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"

In media interviews, Trump acknowledged the conflict with Iran had played a role in his party's losses but stood by his decision to go to war.

Voters rebuke Trump

According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the way the country is headed.

In addition, 70% of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.

"In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump," incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia told supporters at a victory party.

The night included several historic firsts for both parties. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of any US state, while Byron Donalds won Florida's gubernatorial race to become the first Black Republican governor in the US. Democrat Gina Hinojosa will become the first Latina governor in Texas, while Democrat Xavier Becerra will be California's first Latino governor.

Democrats' advances were particularly sharp in heavily Latino counties, including the border counties of Texas that shifted toward Trump in 2024 and the agricultural towns of the Kansas prairie.

In Seward County, Kansas, home to one of America's biggest beef processing plants and where about half of eligible voters are Hispanic, Democrat Adam Hamilton led incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall by 13 points, two years after Trump won the county by 39 points.

An unprecedented Republican gambit to redraw several House districts to make them more favourable largely failed, with Democrats hanging on to most of the targeted seats.

Midterm elections are typically seen as a referendum on the sitting president, and Trump did little to disabuse voters of that notion. In the campaign's final weeks, he held dozens of rallies, telling supporters repeatedly to "pretend I'm on the ballot."

"You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope," El-Sayed told cheering supporters on Tuesday night, referring to Rogers.

Competitive Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska had yet to be called early on Wednesday.

On Tuesday night, as it grew clear Republicans were in danger of losing their congressional majorities, Trump wrote on social media, "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"

In media interviews, Trump acknowledged the conflict with Iran had played a role in his party's losses but stood by his decision to go to war.

According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the way the country is headed.

In addition, 70% of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.

"In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump," incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia told supporters at a victory party.

The night included several historic firsts for both parties. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of any US state, while Byron Donalds won Florida's gubernatorial race to become the first Black Republican governor in the US. Democrat Gina Hinojosa will become the first Latina governor in Texas, while Democrat Xavier Becerra will be California's first Latino governor.

headline: Prince William issues urgent warning as Britons face alarming odds
subheadline: Future King William takes crucial initiative as reign faces threat in King Charles's absence
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Prince William, who has been following in the footsteps his father King Charles and taking his environmental advocacy a step further, has warned about a new crisis for the future.

The founder of the Earthshot Prize expressed his concerns about a “terrifying prospect” of more UK wildfires in future due to climate change.

He stressed that the preparation will be “crucial” during this time and one tragic incident should be a lesson for all.

READ MORE: Prince William takes over for King Charles as Firm prepares for bombshell

William had said this during a visit to the Treherbert in Rhondda Cynon Taf, which was threatened by a huge mountain fire in August. The locals at the time at supported the firefighters to help in time of the crisis.

“We need to start taking wildfires as seriously as the continent has done," he said, noting issues such as a lack of firefighting aircraft.

The Prince of Wales had told the firefighters that this year was the first where he “felt generally worried about the scale of the wildfires in the country”.

He added, “We might go again next season... it's quite a terrifying prospect if we're not... on the ball.”

Furthermore, he noted that the need for “aerial assets” has been pushed up in the government as it’s an area they are lacking in.

The update comes around the time King Charles and Camilla are in Antigua and Barbuda for the final leg of their Caribbean tour.

headline: UN Women honours 17 recipients at Pakistan WEPs Awards 2026
subheadline: UN Women Pakistan organises 2026 WEPs Awards with Derien, Soorty and Geo News as media partner
author: Web Desk
article_text:
UN Women has recognised 17 businesses and leaders for their efforts to advance gender equality at the 2026 Women’s Empowerment Principles (WEPs) Awards in Pakistan, with recipients selected across seven categories from 52 applicants nationwide, including major corporations and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

The 2026 Pakistan WEPs Awards were organised by UN Women Pakistan in partnership with Derien and Soorty, with Geo News as the media partner. The awards celebrate initiatives that promote inclusive leadership, strengthen gender-responsive business practices and expand economic opportunities for women across Pakistan.

Speaking at the award ceremony, Jamshed M Kazi, UN Women Pakistan Country Representative, said: “The true measure of business success is not only what companies produce, but whose lives they transform and whose futures they make possible. When women can lead without barriers, work with dignity, access markets on equal terms and shape the decisions that affect their lives, businesses do more than advance gender equality — they help redefine the economy itself. The Pakistan WEPs Awards celebrate those turning this vision into practice and challenge the entire business community to move beyond commitments on paper towards change that women can experience in their everyday lives.”

The chief guest at the award ceremony, Sindh Local Government Minister Syed Nasir Hussain Shah, said: “Women’s economic participation is vital to Pakistan’s social and economic progress. Recognising businesses that promote equal opportunities, inclusive workplaces and women’s leadership sends an important message that gender equality is a shared responsibility. By working together, government, businesses and development partners can help create an enabling environment in which women can participate fully and contribute to the country’s development.”

Keynote speaker, Nishat Fatima, Chief Executive Officer, South Air, highlighted: “Businesses have a vital role to play in advancing gender equality by ensuring that women have equal opportunities to contribute, grow and lead. Empowering women is not only the right thing to do, but it also strengthens organisations, drives innovation and contributes to a more inclusive and prosperous Pakistan. The WEPs Awards celebrate those making this commitment a reality.”

The ceremony celebrated visionary business leaders and initiatives advancing gender equality in workplaces, marketplaces and communities. It recognised organisations pioneering gender-inclusive policies, integrating gender perspectives into their products, services and value chains, strengthening inclusive procurement and building partnerships that support women’s empowerment.

The awards also highlighted the role of technology and artificial intelligence in advancing gender equality and recognised SMEs taking meaningful steps towards more inclusive business practices.

The national winners will be considered for the regional 2026 Asia-Pacific WEPs Awards, alongside national winners from other countries in the region, subject to regional eligibility and confirmation of the final arrangements. The regional ceremony is scheduled to take place and be broadcast on December 1, 2026 via the UN Women Asia-Pacific YouTube channel.

Pakistan’s champions across award categories

The 2026 Pakistan WEPs Awards recognise recipients across seven categories, with a total of 17 winners and runner-up recognitions.

Leadership Commitment

First runner-up: Dr Muhammad Suleman, SAFCO Microfinance Company Pvt. Ltd.
Second runner-up: Zunaira Omar Saqib, The Square Peg (SMC-Private) Limited

Gender-Inclusive Workplace

Winner: Fatima Fertilizer Company Limited
First runner-up: Abacus
Second runner-up: Artistic Milliners Pvt. Ltd.

Gender-Responsive Marketplace

Winner: Pakistan Microfinance Investment Company
First runner-up: Walee Financial Services Private Limited
Second runner-up: The Bank of Punjab

Inclusive Procurement

Championed by WE RISE Together

Winner: JAZZWorld – PMCL

Community Engagement and Partnerships

Winner: Mobilink Bank
First runner-up: Engro Fertilizers
Second runner-up: EFU Life Assurance Ltd.

Technology and AI for Gender Equality

Winner: HBL
First runner-up: Bioniks

SME Champions

Winner: Davaam Life
First runner-up: Fruit of Sustainability

Pakistan WEPs Awards 2026

The Pakistan WEPs Awards 2026 mark the first national WEPs Awards ceremony in Pakistan, recognising businesses advancing gender equality and women’s empowerment.

Organised by UN Women Pakistan in partnership with Derien and Soorty, with Geo News as media partner, the awards celebrate achievements across seven categories.

The ceremony shines a spotlight on businesses turning commitments into action and creating more inclusive workplaces, markets and opportunities for women across Pakistan.

About UN Women

UN Women is the United Nations entity dedicated to gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls. As the lead United Nations entity on gender equality, UN Women works to transform laws, institutions, social norms and services to close the gender gap and build a world where every woman and girl can exercise her rights and realise her full potential. It places the rights of women and girls at the centre of global progress — always and everywhere.

article_html:
UN Women has recognised 17 businesses and leaders for their efforts to advance gender equality at the 2026 Women’s Empowerment Principles (WEPs) Awards in Pakistan, with recipients selected across seven categories from 52 applicants nationwide, including major corporations and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

The 2026 Pakistan WEPs Awards were organised by UN Women Pakistan in partnership with Derien and Soorty, with Geo News as the media partner. The awards celebrate initiatives that promote inclusive leadership, strengthen gender-responsive business practices and expand economic opportunities for women across Pakistan.

Speaking at the award ceremony, Jamshed M Kazi, UN Women Pakistan Country Representative, said: “The true measure of business success is not only what companies produce, but whose lives they transform and whose futures they make possible. When women can lead without barriers, work with dignity, access markets on equal terms and shape the decisions that affect their lives, businesses do more than advance gender equality — they help redefine the economy itself. The Pakistan WEPs Awards celebrate those turning this vision into practice and challenge the entire business community to move beyond commitments on paper towards change that women can experience in their everyday lives.”

The chief guest at the award ceremony, Sindh Local Government Minister Syed Nasir Hussain Shah, said: “Women’s economic participation is vital to Pakistan’s social and economic progress. Recognising businesses that promote equal opportunities, inclusive workplaces and women’s leadership sends an important message that gender equality is a shared responsibility. By working together, government, businesses and development partners can help create an enabling environment in which women can participate fully and contribute to the country’s development.”

Keynote speaker, Nishat Fatima, Chief Executive Officer, South Air, highlighted: “Businesses have a vital role to play in advancing gender equality by ensuring that women have equal opportunities to contribute, grow and lead. Empowering women is not only the right thing to do, but it also strengthens organisations, drives innovation and contributes to a more inclusive and prosperous Pakistan. The WEPs Awards celebrate those making this commitment a reality.”

The ceremony celebrated visionary business leaders and initiatives advancing gender equality in workplaces, marketplaces and communities. It recognised organisations pioneering gender-inclusive policies, integrating gender perspectives into their products, services and value chains, strengthening inclusive procurement and building partnerships that support women’s empowerment. 

The awards also highlighted the role of technology and artificial intelligence in advancing gender equality and recognised SMEs taking meaningful steps towards more inclusive business practices.

The national winners will be considered for the regional 2026 Asia-Pacific WEPs Awards, alongside national winners from other countries in the region, subject to regional eligibility and confirmation of the final arrangements. The regional ceremony is scheduled to take place and be broadcast on December 1, 2026 via the UN Women Asia-Pacific YouTube channel.

headline: Russia rolls out scholarships to talented students worldwide
subheadline: Scholarship scheme targets talented students seeking admission to Russian universities
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Talented international students seeking higher education abroad can benefit from a scholarship programme offered by the Russian Federation to those who secure admission to Russian universities after winning or securing a position in the International Open Doors Olympiad.

The scholarship provides financial support throughout the recipients’ entire period of study in Russia, from their arrival in the country until graduation.

Under the programme, successful candidates will receive support for travel expenses, health insurance and accommodation costs. They will also be provided with a monthly stipend exceeding 27,000 roubles.

The scholarship is intended for talented students from around the world who meet the programme’s eligibility criteria through the International Open Doors Olympiad.

Further information about eligibility requirements and the scholarship programme is available on its official website.

headline: Iran war played a role in Republicans' losses in midterm elections, admits Trump
subheadline: US president says Democrats would send "insane" legislation to his desk and he would veto it
author: Reuters
article_text:
Democrats capture majorities in both Senate and House.
Democrats flip six Republican Senate seats in midterms.
Results underscore voters' frustration with Trump's policies.

President Donald Trump acknowledged that the war in Iran played a role in Republicans' losses in Tuesday's midterm elections, as Democrats prepared to take control of both the US House and Senate and challenge his legislative agenda.

In an interview with Fox News, Trump said Democrats would send legislation he considered "insane" to his desk and that he would veto it.

"They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them," he said. "And after a couple of months of vetoes, they'll call and they'll say, 'How do we get this stuff done?' And we'll work together."

Trump said the war in Iran had weighed on Republican candidates, even as voters backed his handling of it. "I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran," he said.

His remarks come as Democrats captured majorities in both the Senate and House, scoring sweeping victories that reached deep into Republican strongholds as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to Trump.

The size and breadth of the Democratic wave were still coming into focus, but the party prevailed in states long thought to be out of reach, including conservative bastions like South Carolina, Texas and Iowa.

The Democratic wave underscored voters' deep frustration with Trump's stewardship of the economy and his decision to launch a war against Iran in February, which drove gas prices up sharply. In poll after poll, voters expressed anxiety about the cost of living and anger at the way Trump has handled the issue.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat since the Great Depression nearly a century ago.

In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown claimed a seat that belonged to Vice President JD Vance two years ago, while Texas Democratic state Representative James Talarico withstood a barrage of outside spending to defeat scandal-plagued Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Both Ohio and Texas voted for Trump by a double-digit margin in 2024.

In South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, pediatrician Annie Andrews triumphed over Republican Senator Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham.

Trump elevated Paxton and Graham ahead of more established candidates despite clear liabilities. Paxton has been at the center of a litany of controversies, including his 2023 impeachment and securities fraud charges, while Graham's admitted inexperience drew negative headlines.

Trump campaigned heavily for Paxton, Graham and Ohio's Jon Husted as part of a late election blitz that included more than two dozen rallies, and the president told his supporters repeatedly to "pretend I'm on the ballot" in an effort to fire up his base.

On Tuesday night, as it grew clear Republicans were in danger of losing their congressional majorities, Trump wrote on social media, "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter."

Democrats had flipped six Republican Senate seats in all, ensuring a majority even if they don't manage to hold their own seats in competitive Michigan and Minnesota.

Democrats were also on track to take control of the US House of Representatives after flipping at least eight Republican seats in states including Kentucky, New Jersey and North Carolina and showing strength even in solidly conservative districts.

The party's dominance extended to other races as well. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a three-term incumbent, lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, while Democrats also captured governorships in conservative Iowa and Ohio.

A rebuke to Trump, says winner

"In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump," incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, the projected winner in Georgia, told supporters at a victory party.

In Florida, Republican Senator Ashley Moody fended off Democrat Angie Nixon but was ahead by only about 3 percentage points in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, according to a vote count compiled by Reuters and USA Today, further evidence that even solidly Republican states were shifting dramatically towards Democrats.

article_html:
• Democrats capture majorities in both Senate and House.
  • Democrats flip six Republican Senate seats in midterms.
  • Results underscore voters' frustration with Trump's policies.

President Donald Trump acknowledged that the war in Iran played a role in Republicans' losses in Tuesday's midterm elections, as Democrats prepared to take control of both the US House and Senate and challenge his legislative agenda.

In an interview with Fox News, Trump said Democrats would send legislation he considered "insane" to his desk and that he would veto it.

"They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them," he said. "And after a couple of months of vetoes, they'll call and they'll say, 'How do we get this stuff done?' And we'll work together."

Trump said the war in Iran had weighed on Republican candidates, even as voters backed his handling of it. "I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran," he said.

His remarks come as Democrats captured majorities in both the Senate and House, scoring sweeping victories that reached deep into Republican strongholds as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to Trump.

The size and breadth of the Democratic wave were still coming into focus, but the party prevailed in states long thought to be out of reach, including conservative bastions like South Carolina, Texas and Iowa.

The Democratic wave underscored voters' deep frustration with Trump's stewardship of the economy and his decision to launch a war against Iran in February, which drove gas prices up sharply. In poll after poll, voters expressed anxiety about the cost of living and anger at the way Trump has handled the issue.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat since the Great Depression nearly a century ago.

In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown claimed a seat that belonged to Vice President JD Vance two years ago, while Texas Democratic state Representative James Talarico withstood a barrage of outside spending to defeat scandal-plagued Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Both Ohio and Texas voted for Trump by a double-digit margin in 2024.

In South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, pediatrician Annie Andrews triumphed over Republican Senator Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham.

Trump elevated Paxton and Graham ahead of more established candidates despite clear liabilities. Paxton has been at the center of a litany of controversies, including his 2023 impeachment and securities fraud charges, while Graham's admitted inexperience drew negative headlines.

Trump campaigned heavily for Paxton, Graham and Ohio's Jon Husted as part of a late election blitz that included more than two dozen rallies, and the president told his supporters repeatedly to "pretend I'm on the ballot" in an effort to fire up his base.

On Tuesday night, as it grew clear Republicans were in danger of losing their congressional majorities, Trump wrote on social media, "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter."

Democrats had flipped six Republican Senate seats in all, ensuring a majority even if they don't manage to hold their own seats in competitive Michigan and Minnesota.

Democrats were also on track to take control of the US House of Representatives after flipping at least eight Republican seats in states including Kentucky, New Jersey and North Carolina and showing strength even in solidly conservative districts.

The party's dominance extended to other races as well. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a three-term incumbent, lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, while Democrats also captured governorships in conservative Iowa and Ohio.

A rebuke to Trump, says winner

"In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump," incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, the projected winner in Georgia, told supporters at a victory party.

In Florida, Republican Senator Ashley Moody fended off Democrat Angie Nixon but was ahead by only about 3 percentage points in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, according to a vote count compiled by Reuters and USA Today, further evidence that even solidly Republican states were shifting dramatically towards Democrats.

Democrats held onto three House districts in Florida that Republican lawmakers had redrawn earlier this year, all of which backed Trump by at least 9 percentage points.

According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the way the country is headed.

In addition, 70% of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.

headline: Jailed former PM Imran Khan in good health but concerned about his wife: sources
subheadline: Ex-premier aware of recent political developments, including imposition of governor's rule in KP, say sources
author: Ansar Abbasi
article_text:
Sources describe Imran Khan's health as satisfactory.
Imran aware of political developments outside Adiala jail.
Ex-PM advises pursuing legal remedies through courts: sources.

Former prime minister Imran Khan was aware of the recent political developments, including the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the emergency measures taken by the federal government, when he met his lawyer in Adiala Jail on Monday, sources said.

The meeting, held after a considerable gap, was reportedly restricted to professional and legal matters, in accordance with the understanding that no political discussion would take place.

Sources said Imran Khan was already aware of the developments outside prison, including the recent constitutional and political changes, although the lawyer did not brief him on these matters during the meeting.

The meeting also provided an opportunity to discuss Imran Khan’s health, which sources described as satisfactory.

However, Bushra Bibi has an eye-related problem, which is a major concern for the jailed founder chairman of the PTI.

According to sources, Imran Khan advised that legal remedies should be pursued through the courts to secure relief, particularly in Bushra Bibi’s case.

He reportedly stressed that the matter should be taken up through the appropriate judicial forums to seek relief in accordance with the law.

The meeting comes amid heightened political tensions following the imposition of emergency measures and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the PTI had been in power.

The developments have raised questions about the party’s political future in the province and its strategy in the wake of the federal government’s action.

Originally published in The News

headline: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor 'reacts' to Sarah Ferguson's bold statement
subheadline: Sarah Ferguson revelation about ‘next stage’ causes stir among royals and non-royals
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s ex-wife Sarah Ferguson has dropped hints that she is working on something secretly as rumours of her comeback swirl.

The former Duchess of York broke cover in months after being embroiled in the Epstein scandal with ex-Prince Andrew. Last week, she was joined by Princesses Beatrice and Eugenie attending a memorial service for close pal, Paddy McNally.

Following the appearance, her spokesperson had said Fergie has been “resettling” in UK as she “looks at the next stage”.

READ MORE: Sarah Ferguson breaks silence after UK return: 'In contact with Andrew'

They added that the former Duchess of York had been spending time with her daughters and grandchildren. Moreover, she is “in contact” with Andrew as have “an ongoing cordial and supportive relationship as co-parents and co-grandparents”.

Now, sources cited by Woman’s Day revealed that this bold move by Fergie has worried not only the royals but also Andrew.

Andrew is “even more worked up about this” than King Charles or Prince William, a source said.

“He says his own daughters have betrayed him by choosing to support their mother so publicly while they ignore him and leave him to rot,” they noted.

However, the source stressed that reconnecting with family doesn’t mean a reunion Andrew. It is understood that the two have not met in-person since a long time.

Amid the rumours of a possible tell-all despite Fergie’s spokesperson dismissing it previously, her “biggest priority” for now is “to avoid the association and an interview can avoid all that with a comment about bad judgment”.

headline: Texas turns blue: Hinojosa ousts Abbott, Talarico wins Senate seat
subheadline: Democrats end three decades of Republican dominance, winning governor's mansion and US Senate seat
author: Raja Zahid Akhtar Khanazada
article_text:
DALLAS, TEXAS: Texas has delivered one of the biggest upsets in modern US politics, ending more than three decades of Republican rule in what was long the party's most reliable stronghold.

Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican Governor Greg Abbott in Tuesday's midterm elections. Abbott conceded to supporters in Austin on Tuesday night, saying he had called Hinojosa to congratulate her.

Hinojosa will be the first Latina governor of Texas and the first Democrat elected to the office since Ann Richards in 1990. She is expected to take office in January 2027.

In the US Senate race, Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, who had been endorsed by President Donald Trump. Talarico becomes the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Texas since 1988, and his win is the party's first statewide victory in the state since 1994.

From January, Texas will be represented by one Democrat and one Republican, Senator Ted Cruz, in the Senate.

Final party standings for Texas's 38 seats in the US House of Representatives are not yet clear. Early on Wednesday, Democrats had been declared winners in 11 districts and Republicans in nine, with 18 races still undecided. More results have come in since then, with both parties picking up seats.

Control of the state legislature is also unresolved. Democrats made gains in several districts for the 150-seat Texas House, where 76 seats are needed for a majority. In the 31-member state Senate, 16 seats were on the ballot. The final balance there will depend on these results together with the seats that were not up for election.

Democrats also led in other statewide races: Vikki Goodwin in the race for lieutenant governor and Nathan Johnson in the race for attorney general. In North Texas, Democrats ran ahead in the governor's and Senate contests in both Tarrant and Collin counties, a sign of changing voting patterns in the region's suburbs.

Democratic supporters celebrated at watch parties in Houston, Dallas and across the state as the results came in.

From red to blue

During the campaign, Texas was seen as a state drifting from red towards purple, where Democrats might at best capture the Senate seat. Abbott's defeat overturned those assumptions.

Analysts say Hispanic voters were central to the shift. Immigration crackdowns, inflation, rising housing costs and healthcare dominated the campaign. A pre-election Univision poll found 52% of Hispanic voters backing Hinojosa and 55% backing Talarico, with 56% saying immigration enforcement had gone too far.

Democrats highlighted the human and economic toll of Trump's immigration policies and Abbott's border measures. Republicans defended them as essential to border security and the rule of law.

Debates over religious freedom, statements about Muslims and proposed Sharia-related legislation also featured in the state's politics, though their effect on voters remains unclear.

Impact in Washington

The shock in Texas was part of a wider Democratic wave. The party won control of the US Senate, and CBS News projected it would also take the House, though some races remained uncalled.

A Democratic Senate will shape Trump's legislative agenda, his nominations and oversight of his administration for the rest of his term. The new Congress takes office in January 2027.

The result may also revive talk of impeachment. The House can impeach a president by a simple majority, but removal requires a two-thirds vote in the Senate — 67 senators if all 100 vote. Even with 52 seats, Democrats would need at least 15 Republicans to convict.

A warning for Republicans

For Republicans, Texas means more than two lost seats. It is a warning that their hold on the state can no longer be taken for granted.

Still, it is too early to call Texas a permanent blue state. The state legislature, other offices and the 2028 presidential vote will show whether Tuesday's shift is the start of a lasting realignment.

Abbott-era contracts under scrutiny

As the results settle, attention is turning to whether decisions made under Abbott will now face fresh scrutiny.

In September 2025, the watchdog group Public Citizen reported that businesses and individuals who had donated to Abbott's campaign committee received 89 state contracts worth about $950 million between 2020 and 2024, all without competitive bidding. The same donors gave Abbott's campaign about $2.9 million in total.

The contracts were awarded under emergency powers during the Covid-19 pandemic, border security operations and natural disasters. One company alone, Gothams LLC, received contracts worth about $640 million. Its founder later gave $600,000 to Abbott's campaign committee.

Elon Musk's businesses are also in focus. A joint investigation by The Texas Tribune and ProPublica in November 2025 found that about 1,400 pages of correspondence between the governor's office and Musk's companies had been released, with much of the content blacked out.

During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a temporary pause on new data centre construction and a review of tax breaks given to large corporations.

For Texas's Muslim community, the main concern is EPIC City, now renamed The Meadow, a proposed housing development linked to the East Plano Islamic Center near Dallas. The project faced several investigations and legal actions under Abbott's administration and Attorney General Ken Paxton.

In October 2026, a Texas Monthly investigation asked whether the governor's advisers had influenced those actions. Abbott's administration has said its measures were part of enforcing state law.

Legal experts say the new governor can order audits and the release of records. Criminal proceedings against a former governor or any donor, however, would require solid evidence. None of the reports published so far establishes any crime, and Hinojosa will also need the backing of the state legislature for major reforms.

headline: Scott Jennings fidgets as CNN panel revels in midterm wins during live broadcast
subheadline: Midterm election results gave Democrats a majority in Congress, with big wins in Republican strongholds like South Carolina, Texas and Iowa
author: Web Desk
article_text:
After a surprising night for Republicans, Democrats flipped control of the Congress in the midterms.

The election night unfolded with the Democrats painting blue in GOP strongholds on Tuesday, November 3.

Scott Jennings, a CNN in-house analyst, appeared visibly uneasy while watching a Democratic colleague’s victory lap during a live broadcast.

Jennings joined CNN’s live broadcast of the midterm results on Tuesday night.

As the results started trickling in, Jennings was left with no other choice but to sit and watch his colleague Van Jones celebrating the Democratic wins.

When one of the hosts of election transmission, Anderson Cooper, asked if the result was “bigger than you hoped for?”

Van Jones responded while expressing his delight, “This is like Christmas and a birthday and the Easter Bunny and Halloween.

"This is the repudiation of Trumpism that people have been hoping for.”

To this, Jennings then gave a visible eye-roll.

In a post-election TV appearance on Fox News, President Trump weighed on the GOP losses and linked them to the Iran war.

Trump signalled he would veto the legislation agenda forwarded to his desk by the Democrats.

“They’ll send over things that are insane, and I’ll veto them,” Trump said.

“And after a couple of months of vetoes, they’ll call and they’ll say, ‘How do we get this stuff done?’ and we’ll work together,” he added.

Trump admitted that the Iran war played a key role in GOP candidate losses, saying, “I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time people understood the importance of what I’ve done with Iran.”

Election night saw Democrats win control of Congress, scoring big wins in Republican strongholds like South Carolina, Texas and Iowa.

headline: Prince Harry, Meghan Markle celebrate 'next chapter' in joint statement
subheadline: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex dismiss 'setback' news in new message
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle bid a happy farewell to their years-long team member despite reports that it is a big blow to the Sussexes.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex celebrate the next chapter of Chanel Pysnik, who served as Archewell’s head of nonfiction TV and film until November 4, per Deadline.

Chanel previously served as Disney+ and CNN executive and won an Emmy for her role on Anthony Bourdain: Parts Unknown. Many people saw her departure from Archewell Productions as a setback for Harry and Meghan.

READ MORE: Meghan's 2026 goes from bad to worse with fresh career setback

But this transition apparently took place on a happy note.

In a joint statement, Harry and Meghan lauded Chanel's services, who was one of their very first hires at Archewell Productions...

Chanel "spearheaded the strategic framework for our unscripted endeavours.

"She brought not only her expertise into the process, but also led with her heart in telling beautiful stories.

"Many successful productions later, her impact and legacy at Archewell is to be celebrated. We are both championing her as she embarks on this next chapter."

On the other hand, Chanel also expressed delight at working with Harry and Meghan for nearly six years.

READ MORE: Prince Harry, Meghan welcome major life change in UK amid tough phase

She said, "I am incredibly proud of what we have accomplished, both creatively and commercially, and of the company we have built. I am grateful to Harry and Meghan for their trust and the opportunity to lead Archewell Productions through such a defining period."

headline: Jennifer Hudson mourns Matthew Wright's sudden death: 'Rest in peace'
subheadline: Matthew Wright was 52 years old at the time of death
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Jennifer Hudson is remembering a familiar face behind the scenes after the sudden death of producer Matthew Wright at 52.

The Oscar-winning actress and singer shared an emotional tribute on Instagram, revealing that Wright had recently visited The Jennifer Hudson Show — just days before his death.

“So saddened by the loss of Matt Wright, one of our former producers who helped launch @jenniferhudsonshow,” Hudson wrote.

Read More: Jennifer Hudson gets candid about her relation with Common

“He was just back to visit on Thursday for our Halloween show!”

She added, “He made such a huge impact on so many people in this industry and beyond! My heart goes out to his family and loved ones. Rest in peace, Matt!”

Wright spent 16 years working as a producer on The Ellen DeGeneres Show and later helped get Hudson’s own talk show off the ground.

The program films on the same stage previously used by Ellen DeGeneres.

Wright died on October 30 while working remotely in Los Angeles. He was 52. A cause of death has not been publicly confirmed.

The fundraiser says his husband, Justin, and relatives in New York are facing the costs of bringing him home and arranging funeral and memorial services.

“His husband, father, sister and niece are in New York, desperate to be reunited for a proper goodbye. We’re asking for all of his friends, who Matt loved so fully, to help the family at this time,” the page reads.

The fundraiser also noted that both Wright and Justin had been laid off during the summer, making the unexpected expenses even harder to manage.

headline: Abdul El-Sayed becomes first Muslim elected to US Senate
subheadline: Adam Hamilton wins US Senate race in Kansas to become state’s first Democrat elected senator in 94 years
author: AFP, Reuters
article_text:
DETROIT: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s open US Senate seat on Tuesday, according to media projections, becoming the first Muslim elected to the chamber while preserving a crucial Democratic seat in the party’s fight for Senate control.

El-Sayed’s victory in the closely contested election marked a breakthrough for the Democratic Party’s progressive wing and denied Republicans a chance to flip the seat of retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.

El-Sayed, 42, a former public health official, focused on lowering costs for working families and reducing corporate influence in politics. His platform included Medicare for All, a government-funded universal healthcare program championed by progressives in his party.

Republicans held a 53-47 Senate majority going into Tuesday’s midterm elections, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.

His opponent Mike Rogers, 63, a former congressman and FBI agent, entered the race with strong backing from Trump and national Republicans and had sought to cast El-Sayed as a radical candidate sympathetic to extremism through alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, claims that El-Sayed denies and that remain unsupported by evidence. Democrats said the attacks on El-Sayed relied on Islamophobic tropes.

Rogers also devoted significant effort to courting Jewish voters who may have been uneasy with El-Sayed's opposition to US military aid for Israel and his characterization of Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide.

But Rogers struggled to overcome voter concerns about the economy and Trump's low ratings. In the closing weeks of the race, he broke with the president on the war in Iran and the US trade dispute with Canada, arguing that ending both was necessary to help bring down costs for businesses and consumers.

First Democrat elected senator in 94 years

Adam Hamilton won the US Senate race in Kansas, according to media projections, ousting Trump-backed Republican Roger Marshall to become the state’s first Democrat elected senator in 94 years and helping Democrats cement control of the chamber.

It was a striking Democratic gain in a state President Donald Trump carried by more than 16 percentage points in 2024 and where the race had initially been expected to be safely Republican.

Hamilton, pastor of the country’s largest United Methodist congregation, campaigned on affordability and bipartisanship, calling himself an “independent-minded Democrat” and rejecting Republican portrayals of him as far left.

Wearing a pin that said "love one another," Hamilton spoke in his victory speech of the need for unity between Democrats and Republicans, and for curbing cost of living increases caused by Trump policies like tariffs and cuts to food assistance.

In electing him, "the people in Kansas, Republicans, Democrats and independents, were saying, what's happening in Washington is not okay," Hamilton said.

The race tightened in its final weeks, drawing Trump and Vice President JD Vance to Kansas to campaign for Marshall.

At a Wichita-area campaign rally on October 19, Trump said the US Department of Agriculture would launch a "harvest fuel relief program" to provide farmers with $8 billion to offset diesel costs during the harvest season.

headline: Todd Chrishley defends daughter Savannah over 'gold digger' accusations
subheadline: Savannah Chrisley's dad Todd has a blunt response for critics commenting
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Todd Chrisley isn't letting online critics have the last word about his daughter Savannah's marriage — and his mother, Nanny Faye, had a rather cheeky take on the whole controversy.

Savannah, 29, has faced accusations of being a “gold digger” since news broke that she secretly married businessman Jason Galanis, 56, and is expecting their first child together.

Their 27-year age gap has also fueled plenty of online chatter.

Read More: Savannah Chrisley's dad Todd claims he will never 'forget' them after prison release

But Jason's financial history has added another layer to the debate. He served federal prison time in 2020 after being linked to multimillion-dollar securities fraud schemes.

President Donald Trump commuted his sentence in March 2025.

During an October 30 episode of his Two Sons and Me podcast, Todd, 57, pushed back against the claims about his daughter.

"There were comments today in the press about Savannah's ring, the size of it, that she is engaged to a billionaire because she's a gold digger," he said.

Nanny Faye wasn't exactly scandalized by the accusation.

"Oh, good. I don't blame her. I'd dig, too. If I knew one and I stood a chance like her, I'd be digging 24/7, till I got him," she joked.

Todd laughed before adding his own punchline, saying that if Savannah really were a gold digger, "it would have helped out if she would have started digging when I was paying all these legal fees."

He then argued that critics were overlooking Savannah's own business success, pointing to her clothing line, cosmetics and Good Girl RX.

Read More: Savannah Chrisley's mystery fiancé revealed after pregnancy news

"What do they think this girl has done her whole life, from the time that the cameras started rolling? What do they think she did with her clothing line, with her cosmetics, that she didn't make money? What do they think about Good Girl RX? How do they think this woman lives?" he asked.
